claims.text: At stage-3, OrderItem declares public Vnd UnitPrice { get; private set; }; until stage-2 it was an int property UnitPriceVnd. Vnd is a sealed record with a get-only int Amount and no Id; its constructor throws for a negative amount.

No migration added for stage-3 changes order_items.unit_price_vnd: among non-Designer migration files, only 20260923154631_InitialCreate.cs mentions the column, creating it as table.Column<int>(type: "integer", nullable: false).

A value object has no id of its own, so it cannot have rows of its own. In Đơn Hàng, Vnd is mapped with a value converter into its owner's row: no table or key, its single value is a column of order_items.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (Simple value objects); examples/don-hang @ stage-3 DonHangDbContext.cs:93-95

claims.text: HasConversion(convertToProviderExpression, convertFromProviderExpression): EF Core applies the first expression when writing the property's value to the database and the second when reading the column value back into the property's type.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (Configuring a value converter; HasConversion with two expressions)

claims.text: The column type follows the converter's provider type, not the model type. With provider type int, EF Core (Npgsql) maps the property to integer, as for an int property; the stage-3 snapshot records b.Property<int>("UnitPrice").HasColumnType("integer").HasColumnName("unit_price_vnd").
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (model/provider type; Column facets); Npgsql EF Core type mapping (int -> integer); DonHangDbContextModelSnapshot.cs:123-125

claims.text: The from-provider expression amount => new Vnd(amount) calls Vnd's constructor on every load, so a negative value in unit_price_vnd makes loading that row throw an exception instead of returning an item.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (conversion runs when reading values); examples/don-hang @ stage-3: DonHangDbContext.cs:95, Vnd.cs:12-16; proposed test in repo_changes_needed

claims.text: Loading an Order through EF Core uses its private parameterless constructor, which checks nothing (contrast with Vnd, whose checking constructor the converter calls).

claims.text: At stage-3, DonHangDbContext maps OrderItem.UnitPrice with HasColumnName("unit_price_vnd").HasConversion(price => price.Amount, amount => new Vnd(amount)); there is no Entity<Vnd>, DbSet<Vnd>, HasKey or ToTable for Vnd. At stage-2 the int UnitPriceVnd mapped to the same column name.

claims.text: At stage-3, OrderItemDto is record OrderItemDto(int ProductId, int Quantity, int UnitPriceVnd), and OrdersController builds it with new OrderItemDto(i.ProductId, i.Quantity, i.UnitPrice.Amount).
ASP.NET Core's default JSON options (web defaults) serialize an int property UnitPriceVnd as a JSON number under the camelCase name unitPriceVnd.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: Format response data / JsonSerializerDefaults.Web (camelCase property naming)

claims.text: At stage-3, DonHang.App's models.dart reads an order item's price with json['unitPriceVnd'] as int.

Changing unitPriceVnd to an object would break a client that reads it as a number, such as DonHang.App, and adds no protection when the domain already refuses negative amounts. Opposing view: a structured money object is right when the API must carry several currencies.
